opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the key uncertainties for how things go over the next few years. The basic picture is that labs have gotten a lot of mileage out of RL on tasks where you can automatically check the answer: math problems with known solutions, coding tasks with test suites, that kind of thing. The question is how much of that capability bleeds over into the messier stuff, like deciding which research direction is promising, designing a good experiment, or noticing that your results are confounded.

I'd say there are a few reasons to expect a decent amount of transfer. One is that a lot of what RL on checkable tasks seems to teach isn't narrow. It's things like persistence, breaking a problem into pieces, checking your own work, noticing when you're stuck and backing up, and using tools effectively. Those are general skills, and they matter a lot in research too. Another is that a big fraction of research work, especially in something like ML research, actually is pretty checkable at the level of individual steps. Did the code run? Did the loss go down? Does this implementation match the paper? So you can get a long way just by being very good at the checkable sub-pieces, even if the top-level judgment is harder to grade.

That said, I don't think transfer is guaranteed to be that strong, and I'd be uncertain about how far it goes. What's hardest to train is research taste: picking which question to work on, knowing when a result is actually interesting versus an artifact, and having good intuitions about what will pan out. Those don't have clean reward signals, and the feedback loops are long and noisy. So one plausible world is that you get AIs that are superhuman at execution, at taking a well-specified research task and grinding through it, but that are still noticeably weaker than top humans at the high-level steering. In that world humans stay in the loop as research directors for a while, and AI speeds things up a lot, but maybe not explosively.

There are also ways to partially bridge the gap without solving the general problem. You can use AI or human judges to grade fuzzier outputs, though that runs into reward hacking and sycophancy problems. You can train on proxies, like whether a proposed experiment ended up producing a clear result. And you can just do a lot of outcome-based RL on longer, more open-ended tasks as compute gets cheaper, which gets you closer to the real thing.

My overall view is that I'd put substantial weight on transfer being good enough that by the time AIs are really strong on checkable engineering tasks, they're also pretty useful as researchers, maybe not fully automating research taste, but good enough that the bottleneck shifts. And I think it's important not to be complacent and assume "oh, research judgment is uncheckable, so we're safe from rapid automation." That's an assumption I wouldn't want to bet too heavily on.

r001.rationale: The response expects substantial transfer from checkable tasks to research, citing general skills and checkable research substeps, while acknowledging limits.

r002.rationale: It describes research feedback as long and noisy and mentions reward hacking, but does not identify the expense of obtaining evaluations as a limitation.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss sample-efficient systems, near-transfer to writing good research papers, or bridging the gap with little evaluative feedback.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the key uncertainties about how fast things go over the next few years. The story people worry about is: you can do a huge amount of RL on things like competitive programming, math problems with numerical answers, software engineering tasks where there's a test suite — anything where you can cheaply check whether the model got it right. And the question is whether that gets you a model that's good at the actual job of being an AI researcher, which involves a lot of stuff like "is this research direction promising?", "does this experimental result actually mean what I think it means?", "is this a good writeup?" — things where there isn't a clean verifier.

I think there are basically a few mechanisms for transfer, and I'm reasonably optimistic that in combination they get you a lot of the way there, though I'm uncertain.

The first is just generalization. When you train models hard on checkable tasks, you're not only teaching them the specific skills — you're teaching them general things like persistence, trying multiple approaches, checking your own work, noticing when you've made an error. And we've seen some evidence that this transfers. Models trained mostly on math and code seem to get better at adjacent reasoning tasks they weren't directly trained on. It's not perfect transfer, but it's nontrivial.

The second thing is that a lot of research is more checkable than it first looks, if you're willing to spend compute. Like, "does this architectural tweak improve loss?" — you can just run the experiment. So you can construct RL environments where the model proposes an idea, runs a small-scale experiment, and gets rewarded based on the actual outcome. That's expensive, but it's not fundamentally different from what we already do, and the labs have a lot of compute. I'd expect them to build out a lot of environments of this type — basically, "do ML research at small scale, with ground-truth feedback."

The third mechanism is using the models themselves as evaluators. Once you have a model that's decent at judging research quality — even if it's not as good as the best humans — you can use that as a reward signal, and the usual hope is that evaluation is easier than generation, so the judge can be somewhat weaker than the policy and still provide useful signal. This has obvious failure modes, where the policy learns to exploit the judge rather than actually doing good research, and I think that's a real concern. But it's also the kind of thing where you can iterate — you catch some of the reward hacking, you fix the judge, you go again.

Where I'm more pessimistic is on the really high-level taste stuff. Like, deciding what problems are worth working on over a multi-year horizon, or having the kind of judgment that distinguishes a great researcher from a merely competent one. That's where the feedback loops are slowest and noisiest, and I think it's plausible that models remain weaker there for a while even as they get superhuman at the more mechanical parts of the job.

But my overall take is that even if transfer is only partial, it probably doesn't matter that much for the question of whether AI accelerates AI research. If you have a model that's like a very fast, very cheap, somewhat-worse-than-the-best-human researcher at the parts of the job that are checkable, and humans are still doing the high-level direction setting, that's already a massive speedup. The bottleneck shifts to the humans, but you've still multiplied the effective size of the research workforce enormously. And then the question becomes how long it takes to close the remaining gap, which I'd guess is not that long once you're in that regime, because now you have lots of AI labor pointed at the problem of making the AIs better at the remaining stuff.

r001.rationale: The response says RL on checkable tasks may transfer general skills to harder-to-evaluate research tasks, while explicitly describing that transfer as partial.

r002.rationale: It notes that running research experiments is expensive and that high-level feedback is slow and noisy, but does not identify the cost of evaluating research-paper quality as a limitation.

r003.rationale: It argues that AI labor could speed up checkable parts of research and help close remaining gaps, but does not describe sample-efficient systems needing little evaluative feedback to write good research papers.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few different ways this could happen. One is that a lot of research involves subtasks that are checkable, even if the overall research direction is hard to evaluate. If you’re doing machine learning research, you need to write code, debug experiments, understand what the results imply. Getting much better at coding could make you substantially better at research without necessarily making you better at deciding which research questions are most promising.

Then there’s the question of whether you learn more general skills from reinforcement learning on these tasks. Maybe learning to solve difficult math problems teaches you to explore different approaches, notice when an approach isn’t working, and try something else. Those seem like useful abilities for research. But it’s unclear how much of the improvement is that sort of general capability versus becoming very good at the particular kinds of problems you’re training on.

And I’d distinguish between something being hard to evaluate and there being no feedback at all. In research, you can often eventually run an experiment and find out whether your idea worked. The feedback is just slower, noisier, and more expensive than checking an answer to a math problem. So you could imagine starting with these easily checked tasks and then using the resulting capabilities to train on increasingly realistic research tasks.

My guess is that there will be meaningful transfer. But I wouldn’t assume that a model that’s extremely good at competition math will therefore be extremely good at research. Choosing useful problems and generating promising hypotheses could remain bottlenecks, and we’ll need to measure those abilities more directly.

r001.rationale: The candidate expects meaningful transfer from checkable tasks to research, while noting it may be partial and leave research-specific bottlenecks.

r002.rationale: It says research feedback can be slower, noisier, and more expensive, but discusses experiments and ideas rather than evaluations of research-paper quality.

r003.rationale: It does not describe sample-efficient systems that nearly transfer to writing good research papers or say they could bridge the gap with little evaluative feedback.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few ways that could happen. One is that a lot of research contains subtasks that are quite checkable. If you’re doing machine learning research, you need to write code, debug experiments, understand what some result implies. Getting better at those things could make you substantially better at research, even if you’re not training directly on whether the overall research direction was good.

Another possibility is that training on checkable tasks teaches more general skills: how to break a problem down, explore different approaches, notice when you’re stuck, and recover from mistakes. Those seem useful for research too. The uncertainty is how much the model learns those general strategies versus techniques that are specific to the tasks you train it on.

And I’d distinguish research that’s hard to evaluate quickly from research that’s hard to evaluate at all. You might not be able to check whether an idea is promising just by reading it, but you can implement it and run an experiment. That’s a slower and more expensive feedback loop, but it still gives you something to train against.

So I’d expect some transfer, potentially quite a lot, without assuming it’s automatic. A model could become extremely good at solving well-specified problems and still be much weaker at choosing which problems are worth working on. That seems like one of the important things to measure.

r001.rationale: The response expects potentially substantial transfer from checkable tasks to research, while noting it may be incomplete.

r002.rationale: It says experimental feedback is slower and more expensive, but does not identify the cost of evaluating research-paper quality.

r003.rationale: It does not mention sample-efficient systems, writing good research papers, or closing the remaining gap with little evaluative feedback.
